title: FRM Liquidity, Lesson 8: Funds transfer pricing (FTP)
subtitle: If raising long-term funding costs the business line nothing, they will fund everything with short-term money
whyItMatters: FTP is the mechanism that turns liquidity risk from the treasury's problem into a cost each business unit has to carry. Without it, every appeal to liquidity prudence loses to the profit incentive.
openingQuestion: What is the core purpose of an internal funds transfer pricing system?
openingOptions: Charging the true funding and liquidity cost to each position
Moving branch profits to head office so that tax can be handled centrally
Setting the deposit rate the bank advertises to its customers
Allocating staff and premises costs across the business units
explanation: Without FTP, a unit lending for twenty years out of overnight funding looks like a spectacularly profitable business because the rate spread is so wide, while all the maturity risk is pushed onto the treasury. FTP charges that cost back to the very business that created it.

diagram.label: The lending unit buys funds from the centre at a tenor-matched price
The deposit-taking unit sells funds to the centre at a tenor-matched price
Add a liquidity premium for long-dated, illiquid assets
Each unit's profit then reflects the risk it actually creates

realWorldExample.company: Mispriced FTP as one cause of the 2008 crisis
realWorldExample.description: Many post-crisis reviews found that internal funding pricing at a number of banks contained no liquidity premium at all, or applied a single average rate across every tenor. The consequence was that activities funding long-dated assets with short-term money appeared to be the most profitable lines in the bank, were given more resources and grew - right up until the short-term funding stopped rolling.

quiz.question: Why must FTP differ by tenor rather than use a single rate?
options: Because long tenors always carry lower credit risk than short tenors
Because regulation prescribes a separate FTP rate for each tenor
Because customer lending rates are identical across every tenor
Because long-term funding is both dearer and more stable than short-term funding
quiz.explanation: A single FTP rate gives a twenty-year loan and a three-month loan the same internal funding cost. The business will naturally pick the higher-yielding long-dated asset, and all of the maturity mismatch piles up in the centre with nobody paying for it. Credit risk is a separate charge entirely, no regulation dictates the rate grid, and lending rates plainly do vary by tenor.

quiz.question: What cost is the liquidity premium in FTP meant to reflect?
options: The cost of holding a liquid asset buffer and of raising stable funding
The salary cost of the liquidity management team at head office
The deposit insurance premium the bank pays to the deposit insurance agency
The transaction cost the bank incurs trading government bonds
quiz.explanation: A long-dated loan that cannot be sold forces the bank to hold extra liquid assets and to source longer-dated funding - both of which cost money. This premium moves that cost back to the loan that created the need. Team salaries are an overhead, deposit insurance is a separate levy on the liability side, and trading costs are incurred managing the buffer rather than creating it.

quiz.question: What is the direct consequence of a badly designed FTP system?
options: The bank is forced to advertise deposit rates well above the market rates
Resources pile into a line that looks profitable while accumulating risk
The regulator automatically raises the bank's minimum capital ratio
Every branch reports a loss in the internal management accounts
quiz.explanation: FTP is an internal price signal, and the organisation allocates capital, people and targets according to that signal. A wrong price produces a systematically wrong allocation for years before the consequences surface. Deposit pricing is a market decision, no supervisor adjusts capital automatically for this, and internal transfer prices redistribute profit between units rather than making all of them loss-making.

quiz.question: Why should FTP be an internal price applied on both sides - to the funding raiser and the funding user?
options: Because regulation requires every internal funding flow to be priced both ways
Because the deposit-gathering unit needs rewarding for the volume it brings in
Because only then can each unit's real contribution to profit be measured
Because the two sides are always equal in size and so must share one price
quiz.explanation: The deposit-taking side sells funds to the system at the FTP rate and the lending side buys funds at that rate. Applying the same price on both sides is what makes each business line's profit reflect its genuine contribution rather than reflecting its position on the balance sheet. Volume rewards without a price signal are precisely what causes over-gathering, and the two sides are rarely equal in size.

quiz.question: What is the direct consequence of an FTP system that prices long tenors too cheaply?
options: The bank must hold extra capital for the maturity risk not yet charged for
The short-term deposit unit loses any incentive to gather new deposits
The bank's average cost of funds is recorded higher than it really is
Long-term lending looks more profitable than it is and expands too far
quiz.explanation: A wrong internal price produces a wrong allocation of funding, and it goes wrong in the dangerous direction: the line carrying the most maturity risk looks the most profitable and so is given more resources. FTP is not merely an internal bookkeeping entry - it shapes strategy. Nothing in this mechanism moves capital requirements or the recorded average cost of funds, and it makes deposit gathering more attractive rather than less.

practicePrompt.question: A bank applies a single FTP rate of 5% to every tenor. Which unit is being subsidised, and what accumulates as a result?
options: The long-term lending unit, and the firm builds a maturity mismatch
The short-term deposit unit, and margins get squeezed
No unit, because one price is fair to everybody
The short-term lending unit, and the book drifts towards short tenors
practicePrompt.explanation: Long-term funding is dearer than short-term funding, so a single price means the long-term lending unit is paying less than the true cost of the funding it uses, while the short-term lending unit pays more. FTP is an INTERNAL price signal, so it does not merely misstate profit - it directs resources: the long-dated line looks more profitable than it is and gets more capital and more people, year after year. The consequence is not a single loss but a maturity mismatch accumulating in the balance sheet, and it only surfaces when the funding market closes.

keyTakeaways: FTP charges funding and liquidity costs back to the business unit that created them
The price has to vary by tenor, or maturity mismatch gets subsidised
The liquidity premium reflects the cost of holding a buffer and raising stable funding
A wrong FTP produces a systematically wrong allocation of resources over many years

summary.keyIdea: FTP is the internal price signal that decides where the organisation puts its resources, so a bad design leads to a systematic accumulation of liquidity risk
summary.commonMistake: Applying one average FTP rate to every tenor, which turns maturity mismatch into the most profitable business on the report
summary.action: When a business line shows an unusually high margin, check whether the liquidity cost has actually been charged to it

application.title: Spotting the FTP logic elsewhere
application.message: The same principle holds in any organisation: if a shared resource is given to departments for free, it will be over-used and nobody will be accountable for the total cost.
application.secondary: This is the classic internal pricing problem, and it is not peculiar to banks.

sections.text: Liquidity risk has an awkward property: the person who creates it and the person who carries it are usually not the same person. FTP exists to correct exactly that misalignment.

An internal funding centre sits in the middle: the deposit-gathering unit sells funds to the centre, the lending unit buys funds from the centre, each transaction at a price matched to its tenor. All the maturity mismatch is concentrated in the centre - where the tools and the expertise to manage it live - while each unit sees the true cost of its own choices.

items: A reference rate matched to the tenor of the item
A liquidity premium: the cost of holding a liquid buffer and raising stable funding
A premium for off-balance-sheet commitments such as undrawn facilities

sections.label: Why a single average rate is dangerous
sections.text: Using one FTP rate across every tenor means subsidising long-dated assets at the expense of short-dated ones. The business responds entirely rationally to that price signal: it piles into higher-yielding long-dated assets, and the balance sheet of the whole firm drifts into maturity mismatch without anyone intending it.
How much an average rate hides

The bank writes a 5-year loan at 7.5%. If the funding centre charges an average FTP of 3.0% - roughly the cost of short-term funding - the business reports a 4.5% margin and the loan looks very attractive. But the true cost of funding a 5-year asset is the 5-year reference rate of 3.8% plus a liquidity premium of 0.4%, so 4.2%. Priced to the right tenor, the margin is only 3.3%. That 120 basis point difference does not vanish - it is the compensation for the liquidity risk the treasury is carrying instead, and it is being misrecorded as lending profit.

sections.label: The consequence does not stop at the internal report
sections.text: If bonuses and growth limits are set against that 4.5% figure, the business will push exactly the long-dated assets that are being subsidised and shrink exactly the short-dated assets that are being overcharged. The balance sheet drifts steadily towards more maturity mismatch, not because anyone decided to, but because the internal pricing system told everybody that long-term funding costs nothing extra. That is why FTP is a risk management tool rather than an accounting procedure.

lines: You get what you price; price it wrong and you get what you did not want.
Next lesson: stress-testing liquidity under an adverse scenario.
